## Principles

---

## Index
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/1-principles/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "BreadcrumbList", "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "Principles of Finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/1-principles"}]}
</script>

Everything static in finance descends from one principle: portfolios with identical payoffs must
have identical prices. This track states the principle precisely, proves its immediate
corollaries, and builds the present-value machinery on it.

- **No-arbitrage and the law of one price** — definitions, the proof that arbitrage-free prices
  satisfy the law of one price, and the bound arguments for instruments without perfect
  replicas.
- **Present value and the term structure** — discounting derived from the one-period price of
  riskless claims; forward rates from the law of one price applied across horizons.

Opening pages landing next in this track.

## Prerequisites

Arithmetic with fractions and exponents. The discounting algebra is derived from the pricing of
riskless one-period claims, so nothing is assumed about interest rates beyond their definition.

## What the track is for

Most finance mistakes trace to present-value arithmetic done by formula without the law of one
price underneath. This track does it the other way: the principle first, the formulas as
corollaries. When a real instrument has no perfect replica, the corollaries become bounds — and
knowing which side of the bound a price violates is the practical skill the track leaves you
with.

## Notation used in the track

Cash flows are dated subscripts: $C_t$ arrives at time $t$, and $r_t$ is the one-period rate for
horizon $t$. Prices of riskless claims pin the discount function; under certainty every
multi-period price follows from the one-period prices by the law of one price applied along the
timeline. The track keeps the certainty case and the risky case in separate sections, because
mixing them is where the subject's standard confusion (risk premia versus pure discounting)
comes from.

## What lands next

The track's opening pages land in order: no-arbitrage and the law of one price first, then the
present-value apparatus, then the bound arguments. Each page closes with a self-test, and the
harder items ask which portfolio replicates which claim — the reflex the whole subject runs on.

---

## No Arbitrage
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/1-principles/1_no-arbitrage/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "1 Principles", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/1-principles"}, {"name": "No-Arbitrage and the Law of One Price", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/1-principles/1_no-arbitrage"}]
}
</script>

### 1. States, Payoffs, Portfolios

**Definition.** Fix a set of states of the world. A **claim** is anything with a payoff in each
state: $X_\omega$ in state $\omega$. A **portfolio** is a bundle of claims; its payoff is the sum
of the parts, state by state.

**Definition.** An **arbitrage** is a portfolio with zero cost today, nonnegative payoff in
every state, and positive payoff in at least one state.

The principle: **in a functioning market, arbitrage does not exist** — or more precisely,
prices adjust until it does not. This is not an assumption about anyone's preferences. It needs
only that market participants prefer more money to less and act on it at the margin.

### 2. The Law of One Price

**Theorem 2.1 (Law of One Price).** Two claims with identical payoffs in every state must have
identical prices.

**Proof.** Suppose claims $A$ and $B$ pay the same in every state but $A$ costs more than $B$.
Sell $A$, buy $B$, pocket the difference: zero net cost today, zero net payoff in every state
(the payoffs cancel exactly), positive cash now. That portfolio is an arbitrage — contradiction.
So $P(A) = P(B)$. $\blacksquare$

Everything in this sentence — "identical payoffs, identical prices" — is the engine of the
derivatives track: an option is priced by building the portfolio that copies it and pricing the
copy. The proof shows why no preference assumption is needed: the argument never asks whether
investors like risk, only whether they take free money.

### 3. Present Value as a No-Arbitrage Consequence

**Theorem 3.1.** If the one-period risk-free rate is $r$, then a claim paying $C$ for certain
next period costs $\frac{C}{1+r}$ today.

**Proof.** Suppose the claim costs more than $\frac{C}{1+r}$: sell the claim for $P >
\frac{C}{1+r}$, invest $\frac{C}{1+r}$ at the risk-free rate, and owe $C$ next period — which
the investment repays exactly. Zero cost now, zero payoff later, positive cash now: arbitrage.
If the claim costs less than $\frac{C}{1+r}$, reverse the trades. So
$P = \frac{C}{1+r}$. $\blacksquare$

Multi-period discounting follows by applying the argument period by period: the two-period price
is the one-period price of a one-period claim on next period's price. The discount factor
compounds because the arbitrage can be rolled.

### 4. Bounds When Replication Fails

When no perfect replica exists, the law of one price is silent — but no-arbitrage still
delivers **bounds**. Suppose a claim pays at least $\underline{X}$ in every state and at most
$\overline{X}$: then its price must lie in $[\frac{\underline{X}}{1+r}, \frac{\overline{X}}{1+r}]$.

**Proof.** If the price were below $\frac{\underline{X}}{1+r}$: buy the claim, short
$\frac{\underline{X}}{1+r}$ of the risk-free bond. Cost zero; next period the bond owes its
face, the claim pays at least $\underline{X}$, covering it — nonnegative everywhere, positive
wherever the claim beats its floor. Arbitrage. The upper bound is symmetric. $\blacksquare$

This is the template for option bounds: an option's payoffs are bounded by portfolio payoffs
constructed from the underlying and bonds, and the no-arbitrage prices of those portfolios bound
the option's price — before any model of the underlying's dynamics is written down.

### 5. What No-Arbitrage Does Not Say

- It does not say prices are *fair*, *correct*, or *equilibrium* — only that they are mutually
  consistent. Two expensive mistakes both survive no-arbitrage if they are expensive together.
- It requires the trades to be executable: shorting allowed, borrowing and lending at $r$, no
  transaction costs. Where shorting is constrained, the bounds loosen and the looseness is the
  empirical content.
- It is silent on *level*: no-arbitrage prices one claim relative to others. The risk-free rate
  itself, the level of the market — those come from preferences and endowments, the equilibrium
  layer the portfolio-theory track begins.

### Self-test

1. Why does the arbitrage in Theorem 2.1 need identical payoffs *in every state*, including
   states the trader thinks impossible? (Because an arbitrage is defined statewise — "impossible"
   states occur; the definition is what makes the theorem binding.)
2. Where does Theorem 3.1's proof use that the rate is risk-free? (The borrowed amount is known
   to be repaid regardless of state, so the rolled trade has zero riskless cost and no statewise
   shortfall.)
3. An option pays at least zero in every state — what no-arbitrage bound follows immediately?
   (Nonnegative price: an option cannot be a source of free negative cash. The lower bound of
   §4 with $\underline{X} = 0$.)

## Portfolio-Theory

---

## Index
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/2-portfolio-theory/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "BreadcrumbList", "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "Portfolio Theory", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/2-portfolio-theory"}]}
</script>

Portfolio theory turns "diversify" from advice into arithmetic: with correlated returns, portfolio
variance is a quadratic form, and its minimisation has a closed form. The track proves the
two-fund separation theorem and derives the CAPM from it.

- **Mean--variance optimisation** — the frontier derived by Lagrangian; why the minimum-variance
  combination of two risky assets has the closed form it has.
- **Two-fund separation and the CAPM** — with a risk-free asset, every investor holds a mix of
  the risk-free asset and one tangency portfolio; market clearing makes the tangency portfolio
  the market portfolio; the CAPM falls out.

Opening pages landing next in this track.

## Prerequisites

Expectation, variance, covariance, and the Lagrangian method. The mathematics site's probability
and multivariable-calculus tracks cover both.

## What the track is for

The mean--variance machinery is usually taught as calculation. Here it is taught as an optimisation
problem whose Lagrangian has a closed form — and whose solution's structure (two funds, market
clearing, beta) is read off the algebra rather than asserted. The CAPM's testability, and its
well-known empirical failures, are econometrics questions; the derivation here is what the tests
are testing.

## Notation used in the track

Returns are random variables with means $\mu_i$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$; a portfolio is a
weight vector $w$ with $\mathbf{1}'w = 1$. Portfolio mean is $w'\mu$, variance $w'\Sigma w$.
The Lagrangian method does all the work, and the matrix algebra is kept at the level where every
step can be checked by writing the sums out for two assets.

## Reading the results

Two-fund separation is the theorem to internalise: once it holds, every investor's problem
reduces to choosing a point on one line, and the market portfolio's role in the CAPM stops being
mysterious. The derivation is a page; the vocabulary it explains is the rest of the subject.

---

## Mean Variance And Capm
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/2-portfolio-theory/1_mean-variance-and-capm/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "2 Portfolio Theory", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/2-portfolio-theory"}, {"name": "Mean--Variance Optimisation", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/2-portfolio-theory/1_mean-variance-and-capm"}]
}
</script>

### 1. The Investor's Problem

**Definition.** With $n$ risky assets, expected returns $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and covariance
matrix $\Sigma$ (symmetric, positive definite), a portfolio is a weight vector $w$ with
$\mathbf{1}'w = 1$. Its mean is $w'\mu$ and its variance is $w'\Sigma w$. The investor picks $w$
to minimise variance for a target mean $\mu_p$:

$$
\min_w \; \tfrac{1}{2} w'\Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}'w = 1, \;\; \mu'w = \mu_p.
$$

Positive definiteness of $\Sigma$ is the assumption doing the work: without it, some direction
reduces variance indefinitely (an arbitrage in disguise), and the minimiser is not unique.

### 2. The Frontier Is Two Funds

**Theorem 2.1 (Two-fund separation, risky case).** Every minimum-variance portfolio is a
combination of two fixed portfolios.

**Proof.** The Lagrangian is

$$
\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2} w'\Sigma w - \lambda\left(\mathbf{1}'w - 1\right) - \gamma\left(\mu'w - \mu_p\right).
$$

The first-order condition, using $\Sigma' = \Sigma$:

$$
\Sigma w = \lambda \mathbf{1} + \gamma \mu
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
w = \lambda\, \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1} + \gamma\, \Sigma^{-1}\mu,
$$

dividing by $\lambda + \gamma\mu_p \neq 0$ and defining

$$
w_g = \frac{\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}}{\mathbf{1}'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}}, \qquad
w_d = \frac{\Sigma^{-1}\mu}{\mathbf{1}'\Sigma^{-1}\mu},
$$

every frontier portfolio is $w = A\, w_g + (1 - A)\, w_d$ for some scalar $A$: a combination of
the **global minimum-variance portfolio** $w_g$ and any single distinct frontier portfolio $w_d$.
The two constraint equations pin $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ for each $\mu_p$; the structure above is
what the theorem asserts. $\blacksquare$

This is why "two funds" — an investor holding any efficient combination needs only those two
portfolios, regardless of how many assets exist.

### 3. Adding a Risk-Free Asset: The Tangency Portfolio

**Definition.** With a risk-free asset returning $r_f < \min_i \mu_i$, weights extend to
$w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with the remainder $1 - \mathbf{1}'w$ in the risk-free asset. The problem
loses the budget constraint:

$$
\min_w \; \tfrac{1}{2} w'\Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mu'w + r_f(1 - \mathbf{1}'w) = \mu_p.
$$

**Theorem 3.1.** Every efficient portfolio holds the risk-free asset and one fixed risky
portfolio, the **tangency portfolio**:

$$
w_t = \frac{\Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})}{\mathbf{1}'\Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})}.
$$

**Proof.** The Lagrangian's first-order condition:

$$
\Sigma w = \gamma(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
w \propto \Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1}).
$$

For each target $\mu_p$, the scalar $\gamma$ scales the *same* direction
$\Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f\mathbf{1})$ — only the risk-free allocation $1 - \mathbf{1}'w$ adjusts.
Normalising the risky weights to sum to one gives $w_t$. Every efficient portfolio is
$(1 - \alpha) R_f + \alpha\, w_t$: cash plus the tangency. $\blacksquare$

Geometrically: in mean--standard-deviation space, efficient combinations trace the line from
$(0, r_f)$ tangent to the risky frontier — the line with the maximum Sharpe ratio. The tangency
point is $w_t$; its slope is $\max$ Sharpe.

### 4. Market Clearing Makes the Tangency the Market

**Theorem 4.1 (CAPM).** If every investor holds the tangency portfolio and markets clear, then
for every asset $i$:

$$
\mu_i - r_f = \beta_i (\mu_M - r_f), \qquad
\beta_i = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(r_i, r_M)}{\operatorname{Var}(r_M)}.
$$

**Proof.** Summing every investor's risky holdings: aggregate risky demand is proportional to
$w_t$ (each investor holds $w_t$ scaled by her wealth and risk appetite). Market clearing says
aggregate demand equals the aggregate supply of risky assets — the value-weighted **market
portfolio** $M$. So $M = w_t$: the tangency *is* the market.

Now use the tangency's first-order condition. From $\Sigma w_t = \gamma(\mu - r_f\mathbf{1})$,
row $i$ reads $\operatorname{Cov}(r_i, r_{w_t}) = \gamma(\mu_i - r_f)$ — since row $i$ of
$\Sigma w_t$ is exactly $\operatorname{Cov}(r_i, r_{w_t})$. Multiply both sides by $w_t'$ and
sum: $\operatorname{Var}(r_{w_t}) = \gamma(\mu_{w_t} - r_f)$, so
$\gamma = \operatorname{Var}(r_M)/(\mu_M - r_f)$. Substituting back with $w_t = M$:

$$
\mu_i - r_f = \beta_i (\mu_M - r_f). \qquad \blacksquare
$$

### 5. Reading the Theorem

- **Only one risk is priced.** The CAPM prices covariance with the market; an asset's own
  variance appears nowhere. Idiosyncratic risk goes unpaid *because* it diversifies away — the
  arithmetic of Theorem 2.1's covariance structure, not a claim about investor psychology.
- **Beta is a ratio of covariances.** Estimating it is the econometrics track's regression
  problem; the theory here says what the population value means.
- **The assumptions are the content.** Everyone holds the tangency requires same beliefs
  (common $\mu, \Sigma$), a single horizon, frictionless borrowing at $r_f$, and no taxes.
  Each failure has a named descendant: Black's zero-beta CAPM (no risk-free asset),
  intertemporal models (repeated horizons), and factor models (multiple priced risks) — the
  CAPM is the one-factor special case of the machinery, not the end of it.

### 6. Self-test

1. Where does positive definiteness of $\Sigma$ enter? (§2 — $\Sigma^{-1}$ exists and the
   minimiser is unique; an indefinite $\Sigma$ means a riskless arbitrage.)
2. Why does dropping the budget constraint change *two funds* into *one fund*? (§3 — the
   risk-free asset absorbs the scale decision, so only the risky direction
   $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f\mathbf{1})$ matters.)
3. Which step of the CAPM proof is market clearing, and which is optimisation? (Optimisation:
   $\Sigma w_t = \gamma(\mu - r_f\mathbf{1})$. Clearing: identifying $w_t$ with $M$. The
   derivation mixes them only once, and mixing them is where the theorem's assumptions live.)
4. What does the CAPM predict for a zero-beta asset? (§4 — $\beta_i = 0$ gives
   $\mu_i = r_f$: only covariance with the market is paid.)

## Binomial Model
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/3-derivatives/1_binomial-model/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "3 Derivatives", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/3-derivatives"}, {"name": "The Binomial Model", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/3-derivatives/1_binomial-model"}]
}
</script>

### 1. The One-Period Binomial Market

**Definition.** A stock trades today at $S_0$. Tomorrow it takes one of two values: $u S_0$ (up)
or $d S_0$ (down), with $d < R < u$ where $R = 1 + r_f$ is the gross risk-free rate. A bond
costs 1 today and pays $R$. A call option pays $C_u = \max(uS_0 - K, 0)$ or
$C_d = \max(dS_0 - K, 0)$ tomorrow.

The condition $d < R < u$ is **no-arbitrage on the stock**: if $R \geq u$, borrowing to buy the
stock dominates (stock cannot beat the bond even in its best state); if $R \leq d$, shorting the
stock and lending dominates. Both are arbitrages, so both are ruled out — and the same inequality
is exactly what makes the denominator in the construction below positive.

### 2. Pricing by Replication

**Theorem 2.1.** The call's no-arbitrage price is the cost of the portfolio (Δ shares, $B$ in
bonds) that replicates its payoffs:

$$
\Delta = \frac{C_u - C_d}{(u - d)S_0}, \qquad
B = \frac{C_d - \Delta\, d S_0}{R},
$$

and the price equals

$$
C_0 = \Delta S_0 + B = \frac{q\,C_u + (1 - q)\,C_d}{R}, \qquad
q = \frac{R - d}{u - d}.
$$

**Proof.** Replication requires the portfolio to match the option state by state:

$$
\Delta\, u S_0 + R B = C_u, \qquad \Delta\, d S_0 + R B = C_d.
$$

Subtracting: $\Delta (u - d) S_0 = C_u - C_d$, giving $\Delta$. Substituting back: $B$ as stated.
The replicating portfolio's cost is its price under the law of one price — any other price for
the call, and buying the cheap one and selling the expensive copy is an arbitrage (zero cost,
zero net payoff tomorrow, cash today).

For the $q$ form: substitute $\Delta$ and $B$ into $\Delta S_0 + B$ and collect terms over
$(u - d) S_0 R$:

$$
C_0 = \frac{C_u (R - d) + C_d (u - R)}{R (u - d)}.
$$

Defining $q = \frac{R - d}{u - d}$ makes $1 - q = \frac{u - R}{u - d}$, and the numerator is
$q C_u + (1 - q) C_d$. Note $0 < q < 1$ precisely because $d < R < u$. $\blacksquare$

### 3. Risk-Neutral Probabilities

The quantity $q$ looks like a probability, and the pricing formula reads "discount the expected
payoff at the risk-free rate." It is a probability **under which the stock is fairly priced**:
check $S_0 = \frac{q\, u S_0 + (1 - q)\, d S_0}{R}$ by substituting $q$ — it holds identically.

**Theorem 3.1.** Absence of arbitrage in the binomial market is equivalent to the existence of
$q \in (0, 1)$ with both the stock and the bond fairly priced under $q$; and under such $q$,
*every* claim's price is its discounted $q$-expectation.

**Proof.** ($\Leftarrow$) If both assets are fairly priced under $q$, any portfolio with payoff
$X$ costs $\frac{E_q[X]}{R}$, and zero cost forces $E_q[X] = 0$; a nonnegative-everywhere,
positive-somewhere payoff has $E_q[X] > 0$ — no arbitrage.

($\Rightarrow$) No-arbitrage forces $d < R < u$ (§1), which makes
$q = \frac{R - d}{u - d}$ lie in $(0, 1)$. The stock and bond are then fairly priced under $q$
by direct substitution. Every attainable claim is a portfolio of stock and bond; its price is
its portfolio cost; linearity of expectation under $q$ makes that cost
$\frac{E_q[X]}{R}$. $\blacksquare$

The interpretation is the trap to avoid: $q$ is **not** the probability the stock rises. It is
the pseudo-probability under which risk preferences vanish from pricing — the investor
risk-aversion lives in the gap between $q$ and the true probability, and pricing never touches
it. That is why the argument needed no utility, no beliefs, and no risk premium.

### 4. Multi-Period by Backward Induction

**Theorem 4.1.** With $T$ periods, the price is
$C_0 = \frac{E_q[C_T]}{R^T}$, and dynamic replication achieves it.

**Proof sketch (induction).** At time $T - 1$, each node has a two-state continuation: Theorem
2.1 prices the remaining option at that node, and Δ can be re-constructed node by node. So
holding the replicating portfolio at $T-1$ and *re-balancing* it after observing the state
replicates the $T$-period payoff — the self-financing condition holds because the re-balanced
portfolio's cost equals the portfolio's value at that node (no outside cash). Inducting down to
time 0 gives $C_0 = \frac{E_q[C_T]}{R^T}$. $\blacksquare$

The induction hides one genuine idea: **dynamic replication**. Static replication fails after one
period because the state space grows; but option trading is *sequential*, and at each node the
next step is again one-period binomial. This is why American features (early exercise) are
handled by a maximum at each node — $\max(\text{intrinsic}, \text{continuation})$ — in the same
backward pass.

### 5. Self-test

1. Where does the no-arbitrage condition $d < R < u$ enter the algebra? (§2 — it makes
   $q \in (0, 1)$; outside that range the "probability" is meaningless and an arbitrage exists.)
2. Why is the call's price independent of the true probability of an up move? (§3 — pricing uses
   only $q$, which is pinned by $R, u, d$; the true probability affects who trades, not the
   price.)
3. What breaks in a multi-period tree if you never re-balance? (§4 — static replication matches
   only one date's payoffs; the option's payoff at $T$ requires re-balancing at every node.)
4. An American put in the same tree: where does early exercise enter the induction? (§4 — at
   each node take the max of continuation value and intrinsic value before propagating
   backward.)

## Index
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/3-derivatives/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "BreadcrumbList", "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "Derivatives", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/3-derivatives"}]}
</script>

Derivatives are where no-arbitrage earns its keep: the replication argument prices an option
without knowing anyone's risk preferences, and the binomial model is the cleanest laboratory for
it.

- **The binomial model** — one period, two states: the replicating portfolio solved, the
  risk-neutral probability constructed, and multi-period extension by backward induction.
- **Put-call parity and bounds** — from no-arbitrage directly, with the bound arguments for
  American features.

Opening pages landing next in this track.

## Prerequisites

The [principles track](/1-principles/) — specifically replication and the law of one price — and
conditional expectation from probability. The continuous-time limit is stated honestly as a
limit; no stochastic calculus is assumed at this level.

## What the track is for

Replication is the whole subject: an option is worth what the portfolio that copies it costs.
The binomial model makes that statement checkable by hand — every quantity is visible — and the
continuous-time models are the same statement in the limit. The track keeps the replication
logic visible at every step, because that is what transfers when the products get exotic.

## Notation used in the track

The binomial tree is written with up and down factors $u, d$ and the risk-free gross rate $R =
1 + r$. The replicating portfolio is $(\Delta, B)$: $\Delta$ shares and $B$ in the risk-free
asset. The risk-neutral probability is constructed, not assumed — the track's central point is
that $q$ is whatever makes the replicated price match, and that its existence is equivalent to
the absence of arbitrage.

## What the limit buys

The continuous-time models compress the tree's logic into a differential statement. The track
stops at the threshold and says what is lost: the binomial argument is complete and checkable,
and the Black--Scholes formula is its limit once stochastic calculus is on the table.

## Overview

## About
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/about/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "About", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/about"}]
}
</script>

This site provides free, university-level finance notes in which the core arguments are proved.
No-arbitrage arguments are written out completely; optimisation results are derived, not stated;
and every model says which frictions it ignores.

## The standard

Theorems carry proofs or honestly-labelled sketches. Hypotheses are named where they are used.
Assumptions famous for being false in practice — frictionless markets, continuous trading,
common beliefs — are stated as assumptions, with the robustness question, what survives their
failure, addressed rather than hidden.

## Prerequisites and company

Probability through expectation and variance is the only mathematical prerequisite. The
[economics site's](https://economics.wyattau.com) econometrics track is the empirical
continuation, and the [mathematics site](https://mathematics.wyattau.com) covers the
foundations both assume.

## Not investment advice

The models here are teaching models. Their assumptions are false in the real market, on purpose
and in instructive ways; nothing on this site is a recommendation, and the gap between model and
market is where practitioner skill lives — this site teaches the models.

## Corrections

Mistakes in pricing arguments are worse than useless — they teach miscalibration. Anything found
wrong is fixed and the correction is recorded in the page, because knowing where a document was
wrong is part of knowing how much to trust it.

## Self-tests

Each page closes with self-test items keyed to its sections, written as retrieval practice. The
harder ones ask where an argument used no-arbitrage versus where it used a preference assumption
— the distinction that separates pricing results from equilibrium results, and the one exam
answers most often blur.

## The writing convention

Definitions inline, arguments broken at their genuine moves, and cross-references that name what
the referenced page proves. The static results (law of one price, parity, bounds) are separated
cleanly from the equilibrium results (CAPM) — pricing needs only no-arbitrage; equilibrium needs
preferences and clearing — and the site keeps that boundary visible, because conflating the two
is the most common confusion in the subject.

## The writing convention

Definitions inline, arguments broken at their genuine moves, and cross-references that name what
the referenced page proves. The static results — law of one price, parity, bounds — are kept
cleanly separate from the equilibrium results — CAPM — because pricing needs only no-arbitrage
while equilibrium needs preferences and clearing, and conflating the two is the most common
confusion in the subject.

## The maintenance model

Content is checked by tooling on every change: depth minimums, frontmatter validity, link
integrity, and LaTeX parseability. The pricing arguments carry proofs precisely so that the
tooling-checked pages teach checkable things.

## The network

This site is part of a network: exam-board sites for the school-facing treatments, subject sites
(mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, economics, accounting) for the
discipline-facing layer, and a machine-learning site for the applied layer. Cross-references
between them are maintained by tooling.

## How to report an error

Anything that looks wrong — a replication step, a bound, a definition — is worth reporting. The
fix lands with the correction recorded, and a page that needs repeated patches gets a rewrite,
because repeated patches mean the structure is wrong rather than the sentences.

## The level in one paragraph

The level is the university asset-pricing sequence: present value done properly, mean--variance
from the Lagrangian, the CAPM from clearing, the binomial model with the replication proof. That
sequence is the spine of the subject; the pages are its complete arguments, with the empirical
and institutional layers named as theirs.

## The self-test convention

Self-test items are keyed to sections and written as retrieval practice. The harder items ask
which assumption an argument used — no-arbitrage, market clearing, or a preference restriction —
because pricing results and equilibrium results fail differently, and the diagnosis starts with
knowing which family an argument belongs to.

## What to read first

The study hub's track summaries, then Principles. Everything else is sequenced from there. The
glossary is the reference layer, not the entry point — terms are defined where they are first
used, and the glossary collects them for recall.

## The proof standard, restated

A proof on this site means every inequality and every equality is justified at the step where it
appears, with the justification named: a law, a definition, or a previous theorem. Steps that are
obvious may be compressed; steps that are merely plausible may not. That is the same standard the
mathematics site uses, and it is the reason arguments here transfer to exams and to papers
unchanged.

## The standard, restated

Proved not cited, hypotheses named, assumptions honest, corrections recorded. Four sentences of
standard; the site is their execution.

## Glossary
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/glossary/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "Glossary", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/glossary"}]
}
</script>

- **Arbitrage** — a trade with nonnegative payoff in every state, positive payoff in some, and
  zero initial cost. Its impossibility in equilibrium is the subject's organising principle.
- **Complete market** — one where every state-contingent payoff can be replicated. Completeness
  is what makes risk-neutral pricing fully general; incompleteness is why some risks have no
  unique price.
- **Diversification** — combining assets whose payoffs are less than perfectly correlated, so
  portfolio variance falls below the average of the parts. The arithmetic behind the phrase
  "don't put all your eggs in one basket", and the reason idiosyncratic risk goes unpaid.
- **Hedge portfolio** — the portfolio constructed to replicate an instrument's payoffs state by
  state; its cost pins the instrument's price under no-arbitrage.
- **Law of one price** — two portfolios with identical payoffs in every state must have
  identical prices. Everything static in this site descends from it.
- **Market portfolio** — the value-weighted portfolio of all risky assets; the tangency portfolio
  when markets clear (two-fund separation).
- **Present value** — the price today of a deterministic future cash flow, discounted at the
  risk-free rate: $PV = C/(1+r)^t$. Under no-arbitrage this is a definition of consistency, not
  an opinion about value.
- **Replication** — constructing a portfolio whose payoffs match a target instrument state by
  state. Its cost is the instrument's price under the law of one price.
- **Risk-neutral probability** — the pseudo-probabilities under which every traded asset earns
  the risk-free rate. Not anyone's beliefs; a pricing device whose existence is equivalent to
  no-arbitrage.
- **Sharpe ratio** — excess return per unit of standard deviation; the slope of a line from the
  risk-free point through a portfolio in mean--standard-deviation space. The tangency portfolio
  maximises it.
- **Tangency portfolio** — the mean--variance-efficient portfolio maximising the Sharpe ratio;
  with a risk-free asset it is the unique efficient risky portfolio, and the CAPM's market
  portfolio when markets clear.

Missing a term? The page using it defines it; the glossary collects the shared vocabulary.

## Conventions

Time is discrete in this site's core arguments, with the continuous-time limit treated as a
limit. Rates are annualised unless stated; "return" means net return unless prefixed by gross.
Payoffs are written state by state, and a "price" always means the cost now of a payoff stream —
the subject has one verb, discount, and the glossary exists so its objects are named precisely.

## Portfolio and pricing terms

- **Covariance** — the co-movement measure driving portfolio variance:
  $\operatorname{Var}(w'R) = w'\Sigma w$ where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix. Negative
  covariance is what makes diversification beat the average of the parts.
- **Efficient frontier** — the set of portfolios with minimum variance for each level of expected
  return. With a risk-free asset, the frontier collapses to a line through the tangency
  portfolio.
- **Beta** — the covariance of an asset with the market portfolio divided by the market's
  variance: the CAPM's sole priced risk measure, derived from everyone holding the tangency.

## How entries are written

Each entry says what the thing is and what it is for. Entries never cite a page as their
definition — the pages are the primary source and the glossary is the index. If a glossary entry
and a page disagree, the page is wrong and gets fixed.

## How entries are ordered

Entries are grouped by the track where they first appear, then alphabetically within the group.
Shared terms live in a shared section at the end. The grouping is a map of the site: reading the
glossary's headings in order is reading the dependency chain.

- **Put-call parity** — the no-arbitrage identity linking a call, a put, the underlying, and a
  risk-free bond at the same strike and maturity. Two portfolios, same payoffs, one price.
- **Replicating portfolio** — the trading strategy whose payoffs match a derivative at every
  node. The derivative's price is its cost; finding it is the whole exercise.
- **Two-fund separation** — the result that every mean--variance investor's optimal portfolio is
  a mix of the risk-free asset and one common tangency portfolio, regardless of risk appetite.

- **Risk-free asset** — an asset whose payoff is known with certainty; the vertex of every
  mean--variance frontier and the denominator of every Sharpe ratio.
- **Short position** — a negative holding: selling what you do not own, with payoffs the mirror
  of the long position. Replication routinely requires it, which is one reason frictionless
  shorting is a modelling assumption worth naming.
- **State** — a complete description of what happens; payoffs are functions of states, and the
  law of one price is a statement about agreements across states.
- **Strike price** — the price at which an option's holder may transact; the axis of every
  payoff diagram in the derivatives track.
- **Underlying** — the asset a derivative's payoff is written on. The replication portfolio
  always includes it, which is why the underlying's price process is the model's input.
- **Variance** — the second moment of a return; the risk measure of mean--variance theory, and
  the object the covariance matrix assembles for portfolios.
- **Wealth** — the budget the investor allocates; the constraint that makes portfolio choice an
  optimisation rather than a wish.
- **Yield** — return expressed as a rate; the yield curve plots it against maturity, and the
  principles track derives forward yields from it by the law of one price.

## Hub
URL: https://finance.wyattau.com/hub/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "finance", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "Study Hub", "url": "https://finance.wyattau.com/hub"}]
}
</script>

Finance on this site is built the way it is taught at strong universities: from the no-arbitrage
principle outward. Nearly every headline result — the law of one price, put-call parity, the
CAPM, risk-neutral pricing — is either a direct consequence of no-arbitrage or a theorem proved
from it, and the proofs are short enough to actually learn rather than memorise.

## The tracks

- **[Principles of Finance](/1-principles/)** — present value, the law of one price, and
  no-arbitrage bounds proved; the time value of money done properly, with the discounting
  algebra derived rather than asserted.
- **[Portfolio Theory](/2-portfolio-theory/)** — mean--variance optimisation solved by
  Lagrangian, the two-fund separation theorem proved, and the CAPM derived from market clearing
  plus everyone holding the tangency portfolio.
- **[Derivatives](/3-derivatives/)** — the binomial model as the cleanest laboratory: the
  replication argument proved, risk-neutral probabilities constructed, put-call parity from
  no-arbitrage, and the road toward the continuous-time limit.

## What the proofs buy

Finance is unusually kind to the reader: its core arguments are complete in a few lines. Put-call
parity is two portfolios; the risk-neutral argument is one change of measure justified by
replication; two-fund separation is a Lagrangian and a market-clearing observation. Learning them
as proofs — rather than as slogans — is what lets you see which assumption a real market violates
and what that violation does to the price.

## Prerequisites and reading order

Probability through expectation and variance is the only mathematical prerequisite; the
[mathematics site](https://mathematics.wyattau.com) covers it. The tracks are sequential:
[Principles](/1-principles/) before [Portfolio Theory](/2-portfolio-theory/) before
[Derivatives](/3-derivatives/). The [economics site's](https://economics.wyattau.com)
econometrics track is the natural continuation for the empirical side — factor models are
tested, not just derived.

## What the models are not

The models here are teaching models: frictionless, complete where needed, and false in precisely
the ways that make them illuminating. Their assumptions are stated because the gap between model
and market is where practitioner skill lives — and this site teaches the models, not the
execution craft, which does not survive transfer through a page.

## Corrections and error reporting

Pricing arguments are checkable, and checkable arguments should be checked. Errors found by
readers are fixed and recorded on the page. The same policy covers assumptions: if a result
silently requires market completeness or continuous trading, and the page did not say so, the
omission is the error.

## The exam-board connection

School-level business and economics syllabi touch present value and diversification informally;
the exam-board sites carry those treatments. This site is the layer underneath — the arguments
the informal versions gesture at — and the cross-references are maintained by tooling.

## The self-test convention

Each page closes with a self-test keyed to its sections, written as retrieval practice. The
harder items ask where an argument used no-arbitrage versus where it used a preference
assumption — the distinction that separates pricing results from equilibrium results, and the one
exam answers most often blur.

## Corrections

Pricing arguments are checkable, and checkable arguments should be checked. Errors found by
readers are fixed and recorded on the page. The same policy covers assumptions: if a result
silently requires market completeness or continuous trading and the page did not say so, the
omission is the error.

## Where the site is going

The principles and portfolio tracks' opening pages land next, then the binomial model, then
put-call parity and the bounds, then the road to the continuous-time limit. Every addition keeps
the replication logic visible, because that is what transfers when the products get exotic.

## The self-test standard

Self-test items are execution-first: replicate this payoff, derive this frontier, check this
bound. The verification habit — every price checked against a replication — is the subject's
own discipline, and the self-tests are where it gets rehearsed before it matters.

## The teaching order inside a page

Pages open with the claim, then the argument, then the reading — what the result means and where
its assumptions bind. That order is deliberate: arguments land better when the destination is
named first, and the reading section is where the assumptions stop being formal and start being
economic.

## The one-sentence version

Price = cost of the portfolio that copies the payoffs; portfolios that everyone must hold become
the benchmark everyone is priced against. The tracks prove the first sentence, then the second.

## The line that summarises the site

Price what you can replicate; require a price for what you cannot; know which one you are doing.
The tracks teach the first sentence as arithmetic, the second as theory, and the distinction as
judgment — the order matters, and the hub exists to keep it visible.

## The reading discipline

One track at a time, self-tests before the next page, and the replication check after every
price. The site is short by design; the discipline is what makes the shortness complete rather
than thin.

Finance at university level is built from one principle outward: no-arbitrage. Nearly every
headline result — the law of one price, put-call parity, two-fund separation, the CAPM,
risk-neutral pricing — is either a direct consequence of no-arbitrage or a theorem proved from
it, and the proofs are short enough to learn completely.

## Start here

- Begin with [No-Arbitrage and the Law of One Price](/1-principles/1_no-arbitrage/) — the proof
  needs no preference assumptions, and everything downstream reuses its motion.
- Then the [portfolio track](/2-portfolio-theory/): the Lagrangian, the tangency portfolio, and
  the CAPM as a market-clearing consequence.
- The [derivatives track](/3-derivatives/) finishes the static spine: replication, risk-neutral
  pricing, parity.

## The standard

Every theorem carries its proof or an honestly-labelled sketch with the complete argument
referenced. Assumptions famous for being false in practice are stated as assumptions, with the
robustness question addressed rather than hidden. The [study hub](/hub/), [about page](/about/),
and [glossary](/glossary/) carry the details.
